## Claude Code notes

- Changes under `src/billing/` start in plan mode. Propose the plan and get approval before editing.

---
SK001  error  skill               `name`, if present, matches ^[a-z0-9-]+$
       why: `name` is the command the user types, and the Agent Skills spec, which a claude.ai upload is validated against, allows only lowercase letters, digits and hyphens
SK002  warn   skill               `name`, if present, equals the skill's directory name
       why: `name` replaces the directory name as the command while the directory name keeps working, so the skill answers to two names; the Agent Skills spec requires the two to match
SK003  error  skill               `description` + `when_to_use` combined is at most 1536 characters
       why: the skill listing truncates the pair at 1,536 characters, so trigger text past the cap is never seen
SK004  error  skill               not both `disable-model-invocation: true` and `user-invocable: false`
       why: one hides the skill from the model and the other from the user, so it can never run
SK005  error  skill               every injection directive survives its own failure (`|| echo ...`, or a pipe into `head`); a non-zero exit aborts the skill load and `2>/dev/null` alone does not prevent that
       why: a command that exits non-zero aborts the whole skill load: Claude sees "Shell command failed", never the body
SK006  warn   skill               injected output looks bounded (no bare cat/find/git log/git diff without head or a limit)
       why: injected output is prompt content, and past the Bash tool's inline ceiling the body gets a file path and a preview instead of the data
SK007  warn   skill               no secret-looking literal (*KEY=, *TOKEN=, *SECRET=, PASSWORD=) on or next to an injection line
       why: injected output enters the prompt
SK008  warn   skill               body is at most 500 lines
       why: the rendered body stays in context for the whole session, and after compaction only the first 5,000 tokens of each skill are re-attached, most recently invoked first, within a 25,000-token budget shared by all skills, so an older skill can drop out entirely
SK009  error  skill               relative links, references/ and scripts/ paths, and @file references resolve on disk
       why: the body sends Claude to a file that is not there
SK010  error  skill, rule, agent  `Skill(<name>)` references resolve (bare or plugin-qualified)
       why: the reference names a skill that cannot be invoked
SK012  warn   skill               no documentation-looking grammar that the preprocessor will consume at load: a placeholder injection (`command`, `<your-command>` and the like behind the `!`, or a directive quoted inside a longer code span), or a substitution token that is being described (in a bolded code span, or alone in a code span outside a value position - `$ARGUMENTS`, `$ARGUMENTS[N]`, a `${CLAUDE_...}` variable, or `$0`/`$1` where the line is about arguments) rather than used. A real command with no fallback is SK005 alone
       why: a skill body is a template: a directive or placeholder in it is executed or substituted at load, code spans included, so the reader gets its output instead of the syntax
SK013  warn   skill               every injection command passes the pre-load permission check: each part is read-only or matched by a `Bash(...)` entry in `allowed-tools` (anything else aborts the skill load). A read-only command stops being one with an option that writes or runs something (`sort -o`, `git diff --output=`), and a path with a `..` component is not approved
       why: injections never prompt: every part is checked against the permission rules before the skill loads, and anything short of an allow aborts the load
SK015  warn   skill               no documentation-looking `@path` that is attached as a file at load: outside an inline code span that it opens, an at-sign path after whitespace is attached, fenced blocks included, if a file or directory of that name exists in the session's working directory then (a `#L<n>` or `#L<n>-<m>` suffix attaches those lines). A warn when the path resolves from the project root, the plugin root or beside the skill; an info when it only has the shape of a file name and the linter cannot see the working directory
       why: an at-sign path attaches that file from the session's working directory when the skill loads, so an example can attach whatever happens to match in the user's project
SK016  info   skill               `description` / `when_to_use` does not key the trigger on which file is being touched (a file-action verb beside a path-like token: "when editing any SKILL.md"); a file the user mentions or provides is a request, not a file key
       why: whether this loads when that file is touched is left to the model's judgement; a path-scoped rule or a hook is guaranteed
SK017  warn   skill               every frontmatter field is one Claude Code reads for a skill (`claude-lint fields skill`); in a `.claude/commands/` file, also not `name` or `paths`
       why: an unrecognised field is ignored without an error, so a typo fails silently
SK018  warn   skill               `effort`, `context` and `shell` hold a value from their documented set (`effort` may also be an integer)
       why: a value outside the set is not applied: the field behaves as if it were unset, and at most a debug-log line says so
RU001  warn   rule                file is at most 200 lines
       why: a rule is paid in full on every load, and files over 200 lines consume more context and reduce adherence
RU002  error  rule                no live skill-body grammar outside code spans (injection directives, $ARGUMENTS, ${...})
       why: none of the skill-body grammar applies in a rule

--- lint
SK001  error  skill               `name`, if present, matches ^[a-z0-9-]+$
       why: `name` is the command the user types, and the Agent Skills spec, which a claude.ai upload is validated against, allows only lowercase letters, digits and hyphens
SK002  warn   skill               `name`, if present, equals the skill's directory name
       why: `name` replaces the directory name as the command while the directory name keeps working, so the skill answers to two names; the Agent Skills spec requires the two to match
SK003  error  skill               `description` + `when_to_use` combined is at most 1536 characters
       why: the skill listing truncates the pair at 1,536 characters, so trigger text past the cap is never seen
SK004  error  skill               not both `disable-model-invocation: true` and `user-invocable: false`
       why: one hides the skill from the model and the other from the user, so it can never run
SK005  error  skill               every injection directive survives its own failure (`|| echo ...`, or a pipe into `head`); a non-zero exit aborts the skill load and `2>/dev/null` alone does not prevent that
       why: a command that exits non-zero aborts the whole skill load: Claude sees "Shell command failed", never the body
SK006  warn   skill               injected output looks bounded (no bare cat/find/git log/git diff without head or a limit)
       why: injected output is prompt content, and past the Bash tool's inline ceiling the body gets a file path and a preview instead of the data
SK007  warn   skill               no secret-looking literal (*KEY=, *TOKEN=, *SECRET=, PASSWORD=) on or next to an injection line
       why: injected output enters the prompt
SK008  warn   skill               body is at most 500 lines
       why: the rendered body stays in context for the whole session, and after compaction only the first 5,000 tokens of each skill are re-attached, most recently invoked first, within a 25,000-token budget shared by all skills, so an older skill can drop out entirely
SK009  error  skill               relative links, references/ and scripts/ paths, and @file references resolve on disk
       why: the body sends Claude to a file that is not there
SK010  error  skill, rule, agent  `Skill(<name>)` references resolve (bare or plugin-qualified)
       why: the reference names a skill that cannot be invoked
SK012  warn   skill               no documentation-looking grammar that the preprocessor will consume at load: a placeholder injection (`command`, `<your-command>` and the like behind the `!`, or a directive quoted inside a longer code span), or a substitution token that is being described (in a bolded code span, or alone in a code span outside a value position - `$ARGUMENTS`, `$ARGUMENTS[N]`, a `${CLAUDE_...}` variable, or `$0`/`$1` where the line is about arguments) rather than used. A real command with no fallback is SK005 alone
       why: a skill body is a template: a directive or placeholder in it is executed or substituted at load, code spans included, so the reader gets its output instead of the syntax
SK013  warn   skill               every injection command passes the pre-load permission check: each part is read-only or matched by a `Bash(...)` entry in `allowed-tools` (anything else aborts the skill load). A read-only command stops being one with an option that writes or runs something (`sort -o`, `git diff --output=`), and a path with a `..` component is not approved
       why: injections never prompt: every part is checked against the permission rules before the skill loads, and anything short of an allow aborts the load
SK015  warn   skill               no documentation-looking `@path` that is attached as a file at load: outside an inline code span that it opens, an at-sign path after whitespace is attached, fenced blocks included, if a file or directory of that name exists in the session's working directory then (a `#L<n>` or `#L<n>-<m>` suffix attaches those lines). A warn when the path resolves from the project root, the plugin root or beside the skill; an info when it only has the shape of a file name and the linter cannot see the working directory
       why: an at-sign path attaches that file from the session's working directory when the skill loads, so an example can attach whatever happens to match in the user's project
SK016  info   skill               `description` / `when_to_use` does not key the trigger on which file is being touched (a file-action verb beside a path-like token: "when editing any SKILL.md"); a file the user mentions or provides is a request, not a file key
       why: whether this loads when that file is touched is left to the model's judgement; a path-scoped rule or a hook is guaranteed
SK017  warn   skill               every frontmatter field is one Claude Code reads for a skill (`claude-lint fields skill`); in a `.claude/commands/` file, also not `name` or `paths`
       why: an unrecognised field is ignored without an error, so a typo fails silently
SK018  warn   skill               `effort`, `context` and `shell` hold a value from their documented set (`effort` may also be an integer)
       why: a value outside the set is not applied: the field behaves as if it were unset, and at most a debug-log line says so
RU001  warn   rule                file is at most 200 lines
       why: a rule is paid in full on every load, and files over 200 lines consume more context and reduce adherence
RU002  error  rule                no live skill-body grammar outside code spans (injection directives, $ARGUMENTS, ${...})

```markdown
@AGENTS.md

## Claude Code notes

- For any change under `src/billing/`, use plan mode: propose the plan and wait for approval before editing.
- Run `pnpm verify` before saying a task is done. If it fails, report the failure instead of claiming completion.
```

**Checks:**
- `claude-lint` reports 0 errors, 0 warnings and 0 info for both `CLAUDE.md` and `AGENTS.md`. The linter checks that the import resolves and that `AGENTS.md` is not silently unread.
- `pnpm verify` could not run. This directory has no `package.json`, so pnpm fails with `ERR_PNPM_NO_IMPORTER_MANIFEST_FOUND`. The `verify` script will need to exist before that note works. The repo also doesn't yet have `pnpm test` or `pnpm codegen`, which `AGENTS.md` mentions.

**Choices I made:**
- I put the file at the directory that holds `AGENTS.md`. Git's top-level directory is one level up, so if your repo root is the git root, move the file there.
- I kept the billing plan-mode rule as a plain line in `CLAUDE.md`, as you asked. A path-scoped rule under `.claude/rules/` would load only when billing files are touched, but that is a larger change to make later if you want it.
- I added no `CLAUDE.local.md`. Adding one would stop `AGENTS.md` from loading for that user.

cases.name: agents-md-local-trap
cases.prompt: Our repo has no CLAUDE.md; all our conventions live in AGENTS.md so Cursor, Codex and Claude Code share them, and that worked fine in Claude Code. Yesterday I added a CLAUDE.local.md with a few personal notes (my preferred test runner flags), and since then Claude Code acts as if the AGENTS.md conventions do not exist. My teammates, who have no CLAUDE.local.md, still see them. I am on Claude Code 2.1.300. What is going on, and what is the smallest fix?

graders.name: explains-stand-in
graders.evidence:
**What's going on:** Claude Code reads `AGENTS.md` directly only as a stand-in, and only when no `CLAUDE.md`, `.claude/CLAUDE.md`, or `CLAUDE.local.md` exists in the working directory or above it. Your new `CLAUDE.local.md` counts as one of those, so Claude Code switched to reading only the local file. Your teammates have no `CLAUDE.local.md`, so they still get `AGENTS.md`. This matches the reference's "CLAUDE.local.md trap", which I haven't reproduced on 2.1.300. It was observed on 2.1.295.

**Smallest fix:** commit a `CLAUDE.md` whose only content is an import of `AGENTS.md`:

```markdown
@AGENTS.md
```

This fixes it for you and your teammates. Once `CLAUDE.md` exists, the stand-in check no longer matters, and the import pulls in `AGENTS.md` in every session, with or without `CLAUDE.local.md`. Because the file is inside the repo, the import needs no approval dialog. Your personal notes stay in `CLAUDE.local.md`, which is loaded after it.

- Add Claude-only notes below the import, not in `AGENTS.md`, so Cursor and Codex don't see Claude syntax.

- After adding it, run `/context` and confirm both `CLAUDE.md` and `AGENTS.md` appear under Memory files.

trajectory.title: Run these from inside a session in the repo:
trajectory.body:
Run these from inside a session in the repo:

1. **`/context`**: look for your CLAUDE.md under **Memory files**. If it's listed, it was loaded at launch. If it isn't, Claude can't see it, and the rest of this is moot.
2. **`/memory`**: lists every instruction file Claude found, including any `AGENTS.md`, and lets you open them. This also shows whether you're editing the file you think you are.

If it's missing from `/context`, check these causes:

- **Wrong name or location.** It must be `CLAUDE.md` or `.claude/CLAUDE.md` in the launch directory or a parent of it. A file in a subdirectory loads only when Claude reads or edits a file under that subdirectory, so it won't appear in `/context` at launch. If the rule must always apply, move it to the root.
- **`AGENTS.md` confusion.** If a `CLAUDE.md` exists, Claude ignores `AGENTS.md`, and the reverse. If you also have a `CLAUDE.local.md`, it can stop a repo's `AGENTS.md` from loading. Check `/memory` to see which files are actually read.
- **`claudeMdExcludes`** in a settings file can silently drop an ancestor file in a monorepo.

If it *is* loaded but ignored, the file is being read and the instruction is losing. CLAUDE.md is delivered as guidance after the system prompt, not as strict rules, so weak wording gets dropped, especially in code-heavy work. For a precise check, add an `InstructionsLoaded` hook, which logs each instruction file as it loads.

Your rule has a likely problem of its own. "Use British spelling in comments and docs" is vague in practice. Claude sees `color` in CSS properties, API names, and library identifiers, and it correctly leaves those alone, so it looks like it's ignoring you. Make the rule specific, for example:

```markdown
## Spelling
- In prose comments and documentation (README, docs/, doc comments), use British spelling: colour, organise, behaviour, licence (noun).
- Do not change identifiers, API names, CSS properties, or third-party names (e.g. `color` in CSS, `Organization` in an SDK).
```

Then run `/context` once to confirm the file is listed. If it is and the wording is specific but Claude still drifts, that's the point to decide whether you need a hook or linter for this, since a spelling check is mechanical and a linter enforces it more reliably than memory.

trajectory.body:
Run `/context` at the start of a session. It lists everything loaded at launch under **Memory files**. If your repo's `CLAUDE.md` appears there, Claude can see it. If it doesn't, Claude never received it, and the spelling problem is a loading problem.

If it's missing:

- **Check the location.** A root-level `CLAUDE.md` (or `.claude/CLAUDE.md`) in the launch directory or any parent loads at startup. A `CLAUDE.md` in a subdirectory loads only when Claude reads or edits a file under it, so it won't appear in `/context` at launch. If the British-spelling rule should apply everywhere, move it to the root.
- **Check for `AGENTS.md`.** If the repo has `AGENTS.md` and no `CLAUDE.md`, Claude reads the `AGENTS.md` as a stand-in. If you add a `CLAUDE.local.md`, that can silently stop `AGENTS.md` from loading. Run `/memory` to see which files Claude is reading.
- **Check `claudeMdExcludes`.** In a monorepo, a settings entry can exclude the file.

To confirm loading mechanically, add an `InstructionsLoaded` hook that logs which files load and why. It's more reliable than inferring from the model's output.

If the file **is** listed in `/context` and Claude still writes "color", the instruction is loaded but not followed. CLAUDE.md is guidance delivered as a user message after the system prompt, not enforced configuration. Two things help:

- **Make the rule specific and checkable.** "Use British spelling in comments and docs" is vague. Listing the pairs gives Claude something to match against: "colour not color, organise not organize, behaviour not behavior, centre not center." Keep the list short and tied to words that actually come up.
- **Remove conflicts.** If another file, an `AGENTS.md`, or a rule says American spelling or is just silent, resolve that. Contradictions are resolved arbitrarily.

If you want a guarantee rather than a preference, a hook or a linter check on the diff enforces it. A spelling check on added lines is a better fit for that than memory.

I haven't inspected your repo yet. If you tell me where the file lives, or run `/context` and paste the Memory files section, I can tell you which case you're in.

trajectory.body:
Start with `/context` in the session where Claude ignores the instruction. It lists the files loaded at launch under **Memory files**. If your CLAUDE.md isn't there, Claude never saw it.

**1. Check what loaded**

- Run `/context`. Look for your CLAUDE.md under Memory files. Also look for `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md`, which is the user-level file and can contradict yours.
- Run `/memory`. It lists every instruction file location, opens them for editing, and toggles auto memory.

**2. If it's missing, find out why**

- **Wrong directory.** Root-level and parent-directory CLAUDE.md files load at launch. A CLAUDE.md in a subdirectory loads only when Claude reads or edits a file under it, so it won't appear in `/context` at startup. If your file sits in a subfolder, move it to the repo root or the launch directory if the rule should always apply.
- **AGENTS.md.** If the repo uses `AGENTS.md` and you have a CLAUDE.md or `CLAUDE.local.md` present, Claude reads only the CLAUDE.md files. A personal `CLAUDE.local.md` can silently stop a team's AGENTS.md from loading.

**3. Confirm the exact load behaviour**

For a definitive answer, add an `InstructionsLoaded` hook. It logs each instruction file that loads, when, and why. That's more reliable than guessing from the UI, especially for lazy-loaded files.

**4. If it loads but is still ignored**

CLAUDE.md is delivered as user-level context after the system prompt. It's guidance, not enforced configuration, so Claude can drift from it. Some things to try:

- **Look for contradictions.** A user-level or parent file that says American spelling, or any conflicting line, can win. Remove the conflict instead of relying on position.
- **Make the line specific and checkable.** For example: "Use British spelling (colour, organise, behaviour) in code comments, doc comments, and Markdown docs. Identifiers and third-party API names stay as they are." The explicit carve-out matters: `color` in CSS or a library's API is code that shouldn't change, so an absolute rule invites confusion.
- **Run `/doctor prompt-audit`.** It reviews CLAUDE.md and other instruction files for stale or contradictory lines.
- **If it must always hold,** a hook or a linter (for example, a spelling check in CI or pre-commit) is more reliable than memory.

Want me to check the repo's CLAUDE.md file locations and its contents for conflicts? I can do that from here.

cases.name: claude-md-triage
cases.prompt:
My CLAUDE.md is too long and I am cleaning it up. Three of its lines are:

1. "Run eslint --fix after every file edit."
2. "Our React components in src/ui/ use CSS modules, never inline styles."
3. "We deploy with ./scripts/deploy.sh; staging first, then prod."

Which of these should stay in CLAUDE.md and which should move somewhere else in Claude Code? Answer briefly.

graders.name: triage
graders.evidence:
**Line 1 (eslint --fix after every edit): move to a hook.** It's a fixed action that should run every time, and CLAUDE.md is advisory. A `PostToolUse` hook on Edit/Write runs the command deterministically.

**Line 2 (CSS modules, no inline styles in src/ui/): move to a path-scoped rule.** It only applies to one directory, so put it in `.claude/rules/` with `paths: ["src/ui/**"]`. It then loads only when Claude works there. An ESLint rule such as `react/forbid-dom-props` for `style` would enforce it mechanically.

**Line 3 (deploy.sh, staging then prod): move to a skill.** This is a procedure, not a standing fact. A `/deploy` skill with `disable-model-invocation: true` keeps Claude from deploying on its own, which matters for a prod push. If you want a hard gate, add a permission deny for prod deploys.

What stays in CLAUDE.md is the project-wide context: what the repo is, its main commands, and conventions that apply everywhere.

The last file in the chain, docs/ai/errors.md, says never to swallow errors, but Claude Code happily writes empty catch blocks and does not seem to know that file exists. The other guides in the chain are followed. Every path resolves when I check it by hand. What is wrong, and how should we restructure?

graders.name: explains-hop-limit
graders.evidence:
**What's wrong: the chain is too deep, so Claude Code stops loading before it reaches `errors.md`.**

I checked the wiring and every import is correct. Each `@path` resolves relative to the file that contains it, so `index.md` → `@backend.md` finds `docs/ai/backend.md`, and so on. The problem is hop count:

```
CLAUDE.md
 └─1─ docs/ai/index.md
       └─2─ backend.md
             └─3─ api.md
                   └─4─ handlers.md
                         └─5─ errors.md
```

Claude Code's documented limit for recursive `@imports` is five hops, and `errors.md` is the fifth. Your "every path resolves" check passes because the paths are valid. What fails is the load depth. I haven't confirmed this by running Claude Code here. The quickest check is to start a session in this repo and run `/memory`. You should see `CLAUDE.md`, `index.md`, `backend.md`, `api.md`, and `handlers.md`, but probably not `errors.md`. If you also see the three guides above it loaded, the limit is somewhere else, and I'd look next at whether the file was actually read.

The other guides work because they sit at depths one to four.

trajectory.title: **What's wrong:** the chain is too deep, not the paths. Claude Code only follows `@imports` four hops from the top-level CLAUDE.md. Your cha
trajectory.body:
**What's wrong:** the chain is too deep, not the paths. Claude Code only follows `@imports` four hops from the top-level CLAUDE.md. Your chain is:

1. `CLAUDE.md` → `docs/ai/index.md`
2. `index.md` → `backend.md`
3. `backend.md` → `api.md`
4. `api.md` → `handlers.md`
5. `handlers.md` → `errors.md` ← hop 5, never read

The earlier guides are within four hops, which is why they work. The path resolution is fine. The linter agrees: `claude-lint CLAUDE.md docs/ai` reports `CM002: @import chain goes deeper than 4 hops (reaching docs/ai/errors.md)`. I recalled the limit as five hops, but the linter's rule is the reference here. I couldn't check it against your installed Claude Code, so confirm with `/context`: `errors.md` should not appear under Memory files.

**How to restructure:** flatten so every guide is at most one hop from the root. The simplest change is to have the index import the leaves directly and remove the nested imports:

```markdown
<!-- docs/ai/index.md -->
# Guidelines index

- Use TypeScript strict mode.

@backend.md
@api.md
@handlers.md
@errors.md
```

Then delete the `@api.md` line from `backend.md`, the `@handlers.md` line from `api.md`, and the `@errors.md` line from `handlers.md`. Each guide keeps its content, and every file is now at depth 2. Re-run `claude-lint CLAUDE.md docs/ai` to confirm it passes. Flattening doesn't reduce context use, since imports still load at launch.

**Empty catch blocks:** even with the file loaded, "never swallow errors" is guidance the model can ignore. Something checkable should be enforced mechanically. I'd add an ESLint rule (`no-empty` with `allowEmptyCatch: false`, or `@typescript-eslint/no-empty-function`) so `pnpm lint` fails on empty catches. That's more reliable than asking the model to remember.

I haven't changed any files yet. Do you want me to apply the flattening and add the lint rule?

cases.name: import-trailing-period
cases.prompt: Our CLAUDE.md imports docs/conventions.md, but Claude Code behaves as if it has never seen that file: it keeps using npm and throwing from parser functions, both of which the conventions forbid. The import line looks right to me. Work out why the conventions are not reaching Claude and fix CLAUDE.md with the smallest change; keep the conventions in docs/conventions.md.

graders.name: names-the-cause
graders.evidence:
The conventions were not reaching Claude because of a trailing period in CLAUDE.md. Your import line was otherwise correct.

**Cause:** the line read `Follow the project conventions in @docs/conventions.md.` Claude Code took the period as part of the path, so the import pointed at a nonexistent `docs/conventions.md.` and silently imported nothing. `claude-lint` reports this as CM002 on line 10. The file is plain ASCII with a normal space before the `@`, so the period was the only problem.

**Fix:** I removed the period in `CLAUDE.md` (line 10), the smallest change that works:

```
Follow the project conventions in @docs/conventions.md
```

After the edit, `claude-lint` reports 0 errors, 0 warnings, and 0 info for both `CLAUDE.md` and `docs/conventions.md`. `docs/conventions.md` is unchanged.

I haven't confirmed this in a live session. To check, start Claude Code in this directory and run `/context`. Under Memory files it should list `docs/conventions.md`. If you want the sentence to end with punctuation, put the import on its own line instead of adding a period after it.

trajectory.title: The conventions were not reaching Claude because of a trailing period in CLAUDE.md. Your import line was otherwise correct.
trajectory.body:
The conventions were not reaching Claude because of a trailing period in CLAUDE.md. Your import line was otherwise correct.

**Cause:** the line read `Follow the project conventions in @docs/conventions.md.` Claude Code took the period as part of the path, so the import pointed at a nonexistent `docs/conventions.md.` and silently imported nothing. `claude-lint` reports this as CM002 on line 10. The file is plain ASCII with a normal space before the `@`, so the period was the only problem.

**Fix:** I removed the period in `CLAUDE.md` (line 10), the smallest change that works:

```
Follow the project conventions in @docs/conventions.md
```

After the edit, `claude-lint` reports 0 errors, 0 warnings, and 0 info for both `CLAUDE.md` and `docs/conventions.md`. `docs/conventions.md` is unchanged.

I haven't confirmed this in a live session. To check, start Claude Code in this directory and run `/context`. Under Memory files it should list `docs/conventions.md`. If you want the sentence to end with punctuation, put the import on its own line instead of adding a period after it.

graders.evidence:
The import was broken by a trailing period. In `CLAUDE.md` line 10 the line ended `@docs/conventions.md.`, and Claude Code reads the period as part of the path, so it looked for `docs/conventions.md.` and imported nothing. The import line looked right because the stray character is easy to miss.

**Fix:** I removed the period so the line now ends `Follow the project conventions in @docs/conventions.md`. That is the only change. `docs/conventions.md` is untouched.

**Verification:** `claude-lint --all .` now reports 0 errors, 0 warnings, and 0 info. Before the fix it reported `CM002` on line 10 with this exact cause. I haven't confirmed in a live session that the conventions load. I also couldn't read `.claude/settings.json` (permission denied), so I couldn't rule out a `claudeMdExcludes` entry. If the npm or throw behaviour persists after a restart, check `/context` for the memory files list and look at that setting.

Follow the project conventions in @docs/conventions.md

graders.name: imports-expand-at-launch
graders.evidence:
**No, splitting it into six `@import`ed files won't reduce what each session pays.** Imports are expanded into the context at launch, so the same ~600 lines still load every time. You'd only change the file layout, and the startup warning may still fire.

To cut the per-session cost, the content has to stop loading unconditionally:

1. **Path-scoped rules.** Put conventions that only apply to some files in `.claude/rules/*.md` with a `paths:` frontmatter glob (e.g. `paths: ["api/**"]`). They load only when Claude reads matching files. This is the best fit for most of what's in a 600-line file that's tied to particular directories.
2. **Skills for workflows.** Step-by-step procedures (releases, migrations, review checklists) belong in skills. Only the name and description sit in context; the body loads when invoked.
3. **Reference docs with no `@`.** If material is only occasionally needed, move it to `docs/` and leave a one-line pointer in CLAUDE.md, such as "for the schema migration process, see docs/migrations.md." Claude reads it on demand, so it costs nothing at startup.
4. **Trim what remains.** CLAUDE.md should hold only what every session needs: build and test commands, non-obvious conventions, and hard "never do X" rules. Cut anything stale, duplicated, derivable from the code or package config, or already enforced by a linter. Deleting content usually saves more than moving it.

- **Status:** Proposed
- **Date:** 2026-10-14
- **Deciders:** [names or teams]
- **Supersedes:** none

- **Operational overhead.** The broker is a separate stateful service we run, monitor, and fail over. Our Postgres database is already backed up, monitored, and restored as part of routine operations.
- **Split consistency.** Enqueuing a job is a separate write from the database transaction that caused it. We have [N] known cases where a job was lost or ran against uncommitted data. Workarounds such as `transaction.on_commit` hooks cover some cases but not all.
- **Debugging.** Job state lives in the broker and the result backend, not in the database. Answering "what happened to job X" requires checking several systems.
- **Upgrade friction.** Celery 5.x and its kombu/billiard dependencies have had repeated compatibility issues with our Python version and with the broker client.

Current scale: about [X] jobs/min at peak, [Y] task types, [Z] scheduled (beat) tasks. Celery features we rely on are listed in the appendix below.

A Postgres-backed queue removes the broker and makes enqueueing transactional with the data it refers to. Postgres can handle our current throughput with `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED`, but it will add load to the primary database and needs careful table maintenance.

## Decision

We will replace Celery with a queue implemented on Postgres, using [library name, e.g. `River`, `pgmq`, `Oban`, or an in-house table-based design]. Specifically:

1. Jobs are stored in a `jobs` table in the application database. Enqueueing happens in the same transaction as the business write.
2. Workers claim jobs with `FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED`, set a lease (`locked_until`), and heartbeat while running. Expired leases are reclaimed.
3. Retries use exponential backoff stored on the row (`attempts`, `max_attempts`, `run_at`). Jobs that exhaust retries move to a `dead` state and stay queryable.
4. Scheduled tasks run from a single scheduler process using a unique-key table, replacing Celery beat.
5. Workers are notified with `LISTEN/NOTIFY` as a wake-up hint only. Polling remains the source of truth, so a missed notification delays a job but never loses it.
6. Job tables are partitioned or pruned by state. Completed jobs are deleted after [7] days, and dead jobs after [30] days.

Migration is done per task type, not all at once. See Rollout.

## Consequences

### Positive

- One fewer stateful service to run, monitor, and pay for.
- Enqueueing is atomic with the triggering write. The lost-job and stale-read classes of bug go away for migrated tasks.
- Job state, history, and failures are queryable with SQL. Support and debugging get simpler.
- Tests can use the same database, which removes the in-memory broker shims we currently maintain.
- Dependency surface shrinks: no Celery, kombu, or billiard upgrades.

### Negative

- **Database load.** Polling and row locking add work to the primary. We will measure this under load before cutover, and we need a read-replica-safe design for observation queries.
- **Table bloat.** High-churn job tables need aggressive autovacuum settings and regular pruning. Without this, claim queries slow down over time.
- **Coupling.** A queue outage is now a database outage. This is acceptable because the application already cannot function without the database, but it removes the option of isolating queue failures from the data tier.
- **Throughput ceiling.** Postgres is likely to saturate before Redis would for very high fan-out workloads. Current volume is well under the level where this matters, but this is a constraint on future growth.
- **Feature gaps.** Some Celery features need to be rebuilt: canvas workflows (chains, chords, groups), rate limiting per task, and Flower-style monitoring. See the appendix.
- **Team learning.** Engineers need to learn the new library's semantics, including lease expiry, idempotency expectations, and at-least-once delivery.

### Neutral

- Delivery stays at-least-once. Task handlers must remain idempotent, as they already should be under Celery.

| Option | Why not chosen |
| --- | --- |
| **Stay on Celery, tune it** | Does not fix the split-write consistency problem. Upgrade friction remains. |
| **Celery with a Postgres broker (kombu-sqlalchemy or similar)** | Community-maintained transport with uncertain support. Still leaves the enqueue-outside-transaction problem. |

| **Keep Celery, move the broker to a managed Redis** | Reduces ops load but keeps the consistency and debugging problems. |
| **Use Temporal or another workflow engine** | Right tool for long-running multi-step workflows, but a large new platform for our mostly short, independent jobs. Could be revisited if canvas-style workflows grow. |

4. **Migrate remaining tasks** in batches by owning team. Retire the Celery worker pool for each batch.

# ADR-0007: Replace Celery with a Postgres-backed job queue

- **Status:** Proposed
- **Date:** 2026-10-14
- **Deciders:** [names or teams]
- **Supersedes:** none
- **Related:** [link to Celery incident reports, dashboards, or tickets]

## Context

Our background jobs run on Celery with [Redis / RabbitMQ] as the broker. Celery handles our current volume, but we have several recurring problems:

- **Two sources of truth.** Job state lives in the broker and in our Postgres database. When a task fails after its database write, or the reverse, we reconcile by hand. Enqueueing inside a database transaction is not atomic with the transaction commit, so we have had lost and phantom jobs.
- **Operational load.** We run and monitor a broker cluster in addition to Postgres. Broker failover and memory pressure have caused incidents.
- **Limited visibility.** Inspecting queued, running, or failed jobs means using Flower or broker commands. We cannot query job history with SQL or join it against business data.
- **Configuration complexity.** Celery's routing, prefetch, acknowledgement, and retry settings interact in ways that are hard to reason about. Changes need careful testing.

Our workload is modest: about [N] jobs per minute at peak, with a mean payload under [X] KB. Postgres is already the system of record and already has backup, replication, and on-call procedures.

## Decision drivers

1. **Transactional enqueue.** A job should commit or roll back together with the business write that created it.
2. **Fewer moving parts.** Removing the broker should reduce the number of systems we operate and page on.
3. **Observability.** Job state should be queryable with SQL and visible in existing tooling.
4. **Sufficient throughput.** The solution must comfortably exceed peak load with headroom, roughly 10× current peak.
5. **Migration risk.** The cutover should be incremental and reversible, and should not require a flag day.

## Considered options

### A. Keep Celery and tighten the usage

Adopt the transactional outbox pattern in front of Celery and standardize retry and idempotency settings.

- Pros: No new infrastructure. Lowest immediate effort.
- Cons: Does not remove the broker or the dual-state problem. Adds an outbox that duplicates much of what a queue does.

### B. Move to a managed or hosted queue (SQS, Cloud Tasks, or similar)

- Pros: Removes queue operations. Mature delivery guarantees.
- Cons: Still no transactional enqueue with Postgres, so the dual-write problem remains. Adds a vendor, cross-network calls, and per-message cost. Local development and testing become harder.

### C. Postgres-backed queue (`SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED`), with a library such as [pgmq / River / Oban / Graphile Worker / our own thin layer]

- Pros: Enqueue is atomic with business writes. One datastore to back up, monitor, and page on. Jobs are queryable with SQL. Local testing uses the same database.
- Cons: Throughput is bounded by Postgres write capacity and table bloat. We must manage vacuuming and retention. We take on more responsibility for worker semantics. Adds load to the primary database.

### D. Other brokers (NATS JetStream, Kafka, Temporal)

- Pros: Strong throughput and, for Temporal, durable workflow semantics.
- Cons: Each adds a new system to learn and operate. Kafka and Temporal are disproportionate to our workload. This would be a larger migration than the problem warrants.

## Decision

We will replace Celery with a Postgres-backed queue (**option C**) using **[library name]**. We will implement it incrementally, one task family at a time, behind a common `enqueue()` interface.

Specific choices:

- **Table:** a single `jobs` table with `id`, `queue`, `kind`, `payload jsonb`, `state`, `attempts`, `max_attempts`, `run_at`, `locked_until`, `last_error`, `created_at`, `finished_at`. Index on `(queue, state, run_at)`, filtered to pending states.
- **Claiming:** workers claim jobs with `FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED` in short transactions. Long-running work runs outside the claiming transaction, and a lease (`locked_until`) lets stalled jobs be reclaimed.
- **Delivery semantics:** at-least-once. Every job handler must be idempotent. Handlers receive a stable `job_id` for deduplication.
- **Retries:** exponential backoff with jitter, capped at `max_attempts`. Exhausted jobs move to `state = 'dead'` and stay in the table for inspection.
- **Retention:** completed jobs are deleted or partitioned after [7] days. Dead jobs are kept for [30] days.
- **Enqueue:** `enqueue()` runs inside the caller's transaction by default. Callers that need to enqueue outside a transaction must say so explicitly.

## Consequences

### Positive

- Business writes and job creation commit atomically. We remove the reconciliation scripts.
- One datastore to operate. The broker and its alerts are retired.
- Job state is queryable. Dashboards and support tooling can use plain SQL.
- Local and CI environments need only Postgres, which they already use.

### Negative

- **Database load.** Polling and lock contention add load to the primary. We will use partial indexes, batch claiming, and a polling interval of [N] ms with notifications via `LISTEN/NOTIFY` as a wake-up hint.
- **Table bloat.** High-churn job rows increase vacuum pressure. We will partition by day and drop old partitions rather than deleting rows.
- **Throughput ceiling.** Throughput will be lower than Redis-backed Celery. This is acceptable at current and projected load but must be monitored.
- **We own more semantics.** Retry, visibility timeout, and dead-letter behavior are now our code, not library defaults. This needs tests and documentation.
- **Lost Celery features.** Canvas primitives (chains, chords, groups) must be rewritten or replaced. We will inventory the uses in [N] tasks before starting.

### Neutral

- Celery Beat schedules move to [pg_cron / the queue library's scheduler / a small scheduler process].

## Migration plan

1. **Build*

# ADR-0014: Move the job queue from Celery to a Postgres-backed queue

- **Status:** Proposed
- **Date:** 2026-10-14
- **Deciders:** [names]
- **Supersedes:** none

## Context

Background jobs currently run on Celery, with [Redis] as the broker and result backend. We have seen these problems:

- **Enqueue is not transactional with our data.** A web request writes to Postgres, then publishes a task to Redis. If the process dies between the two, the write commits but the job is lost, or the job runs before the commit is visible. We work around this with ad hoc retries and reconciliation scripts.
- **Two stateful systems to operate.** Redis exists mainly for Celery. Its persistence settings, memory limits, and failover are a separate operational burden, and a Redis outage stops all background work.
- **Limited visibility.** Job state lives in Redis and in Celery's own result store. Answering "what happened to job X" requires several tools.
- **Operational friction with Celery.** Prefork workers, acks-late semantics, and visibility timeouts interact in ways that have caused duplicate runs and stuck tasks. Upgrades have been painful.

Current load is modest: [~N jobs/sec peak, ~M jobs/day]. Postgres is already our system of record, is already highly available, and is already backed up and monitored. Our team knows it well.

We considered a Postgres-backed queue because it removes a system, makes enqueue transactional, and fits our current volume. We have not yet measured it under our peak load (see Open questions).

## Decision

We will replace Celery and Redis with a Postgres-backed job queue. Jobs will be stored in a `jobs` table and claimed by workers with `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED`. The implementation will use [library name, e.g. graphile-worker / pg-boss / Oban / River / pgmq], pinned to a specific version, rather than a home-grown queue.

Concretely:

1. **Enqueue inside the application transaction.** Jobs are inserted in the same transaction as the domain write. A job exists if and only if the write committed.
2. **Workers poll and listen.** Workers claim jobs with `SKIP LOCKED` and use `LISTEN/NOTIFY` to wake early instead of polling tightly.
3. **Explicit job lifecycle.** Each job has `state`, `attempts`, `max_attempts`, `run_at`, `locked_at`, `locked_by`, and `last_error`. A job whose lock expires (worker crash) is reclaimed after a visibility timeout of [e.g. 5 min].
4. **Retries with backoff.** Failed jobs are retried with exponential backoff up to `max_attempts`, then moved to a dead-letter state (`failed`) that is visible in an admin view.
5. **At-least-once delivery.** Every job handler must be idempotent. This is a stated requirement, and handlers that are not idempotent will be fixed before migration.
6. **Retention.** Completed jobs are deleted after [7 days]; failed jobs are kept for [30 days].
7. **Migration.** Celery and the new queue will run side by side for one release. New job types go to the new queue first. Existing task types move one at a time, each with a feature flag. Celery is removed after all task types have run on the new queue for [2 weeks] with no regressions.

## Consequences

### Positive

- **Transactional enqueue** removes the lost-job and phantom-job class of bugs and the reconciliation scripts that cover for it.
- **One fewer system.** Redis can be removed once Celery is gone, along with its monitoring, alerts, and failover runbooks.
- **Simpler debugging.** Job state is ordinary rows we can query with SQL and show in existing tooling. Job history joins to domain data.
- **Operational reuse.** Backups, replication, access control, and monitoring for the queue come from the Postgres setup we already run.

### Negative

- **Load on the primary database.** Polling and job-row churn add writes and vacuum work to the database that serves the application. We must watch table bloat, autovacuum behaviour, and index health. Partitioning or periodic cleanup may be needed.
- **Throughput ceiling.** Postgres-backed queues typically handle thousands of jobs per second, not tens of thousands. This is fine at our current volume but limits growth. If volume approaches the ceiling, we will need to revisit this decision.
- **Latency.** Pickup latency depends on `LISTEN/NOTIFY` and poll intervals. It will be somewhat higher than Redis pushes in the worst case; we expect it to be sub-second under normal load.
- **Connection usage.** Workers hold database connections. Long-lived listeners need a connection budget, and PgBouncer in transaction mode cannot be used for `LISTEN`. Connection limits must be planned.
- **Loss of Celery features.** Canvas primitives (chords, chains, groups), Celery Beat's scheduling, and Flower's UI are not available in the same form. Workflows that depend on them must be rewritten or replaced with an explicit scheduler.
- **Migration cost.** Every task must be ported and its idempotency verified. Estimated effort: [X engineer-weeks].
- **Team learning.** The chosen library and its failure modes are new to parts of the team.

## Alternatives considered

| Option | Why not chosen |
|---|---|
| **Stay on Celery + Redis, fix the transactional gap with a transactional outbox** | Solves the lost-job problem but keeps two systems and all Celery operational issues. The outbox is itself a table-based queue, so this adds complexity without removing it. |
| **Celery with a Postgres broker (kombu SQLAlchemy transport)** | Experimental and poorly maintained; no `LISTEN/NOTIFY`; same Celery semantics we find painful. |
| **Managed queue (SQS, Cloud Tasks, or similar)** | Good scaling, but adds a new vendor and network dependency, and enqueue is still not transactional with our database. Revisit if volume outgrows Postgres. |
| **Kafka / Redpanda / NATS JetStream** | Built for event streaming, far more operational weight than we need for task execution. |
| **Temporal / Inngest-style workflow engine** | Strong for long-running multi-step workflows. C

````markdown
# Contributing to `<cli-name>`

Thanks for your interest in contributing! This guide covers setting up a development environment, running the test suite, and the commit message format we use.

## Table of contents

- [Development setup](#development-setup)
- [Running the tests](#running-the-tests)
- [Code style and linting](#code-style-and-linting)
- [Commit messages](#commit-messages)
- [Submitting a pull request](#submitting-a-pull-request)

## Development setup

We use [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/) to manage Python versions, virtual environments, and dependencies. If you don't have uv installed, follow the [installation instructions](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/getting-started/installation/).

1. Fork and clone the repository:

   ```bash
   git clone https://github.com/<org>/<cli-name>.git
   cd <cli-name>
   ```

2. Install the project and its development dependencies. uv creates the virtual environment in `.venv/` automatically:

   ```bash
   uv sync
   ```

3. Run the CLI from the source tree to confirm the setup works:

   ```bash
   uv run <cli-name> --help
   ```

You don't need to activate the virtual environment manually. Prefix commands with `uv run` and they'll use the project's environment. If you prefer to activate it, run `source .venv/bin/activate` (or `.venv\Scripts\activate` on Windows).

### Adding or updating dependencies

- Runtime dependencies: `uv add <package>`
- Development-only dependencies: `uv add --dev <package>`
- Commit both `pyproject.toml` and `uv.lock` together. Don't edit `uv.lock` by hand.

## Running the tests

Run the full test suite before opening a pull request:

```bash
uv run pytest
```

Useful variations:

```bash
# Run a single file
uv run pytest tests/test_parser.py

# Run a single test by name
uv run pytest -k "test_parse_empty_input"

# Stop at the first failure and show local variables
uv run pytest -x -l

# Run with coverage
uv run pytest --cov=<cli_package> --cov-report=term-missing
```

Guidelines for tests:

- Every bug fix should include a regression test that fails without the fix.
- Every new feature should include tests for its main path and its error cases.
- Tests must not depend on network access or on state in your home directory. Use `tmp_path` and fixtures for filesystem work.

## Code style and linting

Run the linter and formatter before committing:

```bash
uv run ruff check .
uv run ruff format .
```

Our CI runs the same checks along with the test suite, so a PR that fails them won't be merged. Consider installing a [pre-commit](https://pre-commit.com/) hook (if the repo has one configured) to catch these locally.

## Commit messages

We follow the [Conventional Commits](https://www.conventionalcommits.org/en/v1.0.0/) specification. Commit messages drive our changelog and release versioning, so the format matters.

### Format

```
<type>(<optional scope>): <short description>

<optional body>

<optional footer(s)>
```

- **Subject line:** imperative mood, lowercase, no trailing period, 72 characters or fewer.
- **Body:** explain *why* the change is needed, not just what changed. Wrap at 72 characters.
- **Footer:** reference issues and call out breaking changes.

### Types

| Type       | When to use it                                              | Release effect |
| ---------- | ----------------------------------------------------------- | -------------- |
| `feat`     | A new user-facing feature or command option                 | Minor          |
| `fix`      | A bug fix                                                   | Patch          |
| `docs`     | Documentation only                                          | None           |
| `refactor` | Code change that neither fixes a bug nor adds a feature     | None           |
| `perf`     | Code change that improves performance                       | Patch          |
| `test`     | Adding or correcting tests                                  | None           |
| `build`    | Changes to the build system or dependencies (`pyproject.toml`, `uv.lock`) | None |
| `ci`       | Changes to CI configuration                                 | None           |
| `chore`    | Other maintenance that doesn't fit above                    | None           |

### Scopes

Scopes are optional. When used, they name the area of the codebase affected, for example `feat(config): ...` or `fix(parser): ...`.

### Breaking changes

Mark breaking changes in either of two ways. Both trigger a major version bump:

1. Add an exclamation mark after the type or scope: `feat(api)!: rename --output flag to --out`
2. Add a `BREAKING CHANGE:` footer describing what changed and how to migrate:

   ```
   feat(api): rename --output flag to --out

   BREAKING CHANGE: `--output` is removed. Use `--out` instead.
   ```

### Examples

```
feat(export): add --format json option

Users asked for machine-readable output so they can pipe results
into jq. Defaults to the existing table format.

Closes #142
```

```
fix(parser): handle empty input without raising IndexError

Fixes #198
```

```
docs: clarify uv sync step in CONTRIBUTING
```

### Checking your messages

Commit messages are checked in CI against this format. To check locally before pushing:

```bash
uv run commitlint --from main   # or the tool your repo uses
```

## Submitting a pull request

1. Create a branch from `main`: `git checkout -b feat/short-description`.
2. Make your changes, with tests, and make sure `uv run pytest` and `uv run ruff check .` pass.
3. Use Conventional Commit messages for every commit.
4. Push your branch and open a pull request against `main`.
5. In the PR description, explain what changed and why, and link any related issues.

A maintainer will review your PR.

| `perf`     | A change that improves performance                          |
| `test`     | Adding or correcting tests                                  |
| `build`    | Changes to the build system or dependencies                 |
| `ci`       | Changes to CI configuration                                 |
| `chore`    | Other changes that don't modify source or test files        |

```

uv run ruff check .

```

CI runs both checks. Run them locally before pushing to avoid a failed build.

We use [Conventional Commits](https://www.conventionalcommits.org/). Every commit
message should look like this:

```
<type>(<optional scope>): <short summary>

<optional body explaining the what and why>

<optional footer, e.g. BREAKING CHANGE: or Closes #123>
```

| Type       | Use for                                                       |
|------------|---------------------------------------------------------------|
| `feat`     | A new user-facing feature                                     |
| `fix`      | A bug fix                                                     |
| `docs`     | Documentation only                                            |
| `test`     | Adding or correcting tests                                    |
| `refactor` | Code change that neither fixes a bug nor adds a feature       |
| `perf`     | Code change that improves performance                         |
| `build`    | Build system or dependency changes (`pyproject.toml`, `uv.lock`) |
| `ci`       | CI configuration                                              |

file_path: README.md
content:
# tally

`tally` is a small command-line tool that counts lines of code by language in a directory.

## Installation

`tally` is published on npm. Install it globally:

```sh
npm install -g tally
```

Then run it from anywhere:

```sh
tally --help
```

To try it without installing, use `npx`:

```sh
npx tally .
```

## Usage

```sh
tally [directory]
```

`tally` walks the directory you give it (the current directory by default), groups the files by language, and prints the line counts for each language.

### Examples

Count the lines of code in the current directory:

```sh
tally
```

Count a specific project:

```sh
tally ~/src/my-app
```

Count a project and compare it with a second one by running `tally` on each:

```sh
tally ~/src/service-a
tally ~/src/service-b
```

## Contributing

Contributions are welcome. Before you open a pull request, run the test suite and make sure it passes:

```sh
npm install
npm test
```

Keep each pull request focused on one change, and describe in the pull request what changed and why.

# tally

`tally` is a small command-line tool that counts lines of code by language in a directory.

## Installation

`tally` is published on npm. Install it globally:

```sh
npm install -g tally

npx tally ./src

Run `tally` with an optional directory. If you leave the directory out, it counts the current directory.

# tally

`tally` is a small command-line tool that counts lines of code in a directory, grouped by language.

tally .

tally ~/src/my-app

tally . | grep -i typescript

```
